en: The Sūtra on Turning the Wheel of Dharma, translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī, seated beneath the tree of the Deer Park. At that time...
There were a thousand bhikṣus and various devas, all gathered in a great assembly that filled the air; at that time, a natural Dharma-wheel flew forth and revolved before the Buddha.
The Buddha stroked the wheel with his hand and said: "Stop!

In the past, for countless kalpas, I have transmigrated because of name-and-form and undergone immeasurable suffering. Now, the mind of delusion and craving has ceased; the fetters of outflows have been untied; the faculties are stilled and birth-and-death are severed; I shall no longer transmigrate through the five realms."
The wheel then stopped.
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are two things in the world that lead to extreme conduct; disciples who have gone forth from the home life should never engage in them for as long as they live.”
What are these two?
First, the mind dwells upon desire and lacks the will for purity; second, one is attached to the affection for the body and is unable to practice with diligence.
For this reason, one retreats from the path and fails to encounter a Buddha or a person endowed with the Way and its Virtue.

If this bhikṣu does not dwell on thoughts of sensual desire or the practice of attachment to the body, he may attain the middle way; the Tathāgata, the Most Perfectly Awakened One, has attained the eye and attained wisdom, crossing over from both extremes and personally reaching Nirvāṇa.
What is meant by "receiving the middle"?

It refers to receiving the Eightfold Noble Path: first, right view; second, right intention; third, right speech; fourth, right action; fifth, right livelihood; sixth, right effort; seventh, right mindfulness; and eighth, right concentration.

If monks have heard the Way from beginning to end, they should already know that "this is the noble truth of suffering," having received it with a single mind through vision, meditative reflection, wisdom, and insight; they should awaken their thoughts and cause the mind to be liberated. They should know that "this is the noble truth of the origin and cessation of suffering," having received it through vision, contemplation, wisdom, and insight; they should awaken their thoughts and cause the mind to be liberated. Such is the truth of cessation.
What is called suffering?

It refers to the suffering of birth and old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of grief, lamentation, and despair, the suffering of association with the disliked, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and, fundamentally, the suffering that arises from the intense accumulation of the five aggregates.
What is the origin of suffering?

It is that from craving there arises the nature of renewed existence; not being free from attachment and delight wherever they may be—namely, craving for sense-desires, craving for form, and craving for the formless—this is the origin of suffering.
What is called the exhaustion of suffering?

It means awakening to the fact that from craving there arises further delight; one does not accept lustful thoughts, does not dwell on them, and being without remainder and without lust, one relinquishes them so that no further meditative absorption remains—this is the cultivation of exhaustion.
What is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?

It refers to the practice of the Eightfold Noble Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
"Furthermore, monks! That 'suffering' is the noble truth;

that 'the origin of suffering' is the noble truth; that 'the cessation of the origin of suffering' is the noble truth; and that 'the path leading to the cessation of the origin of suffering' is the noble truth—if one has not previously heard these teachings, one shall receive the eye, receive vision through meditation, receive wisdom, receive insight, and receive mindfulness, so that the mind may attain liberation."

If those who are here have not yet heard this Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, they shall receive the eye of the Path, receive meditative reflection, and receive the awakening of wisdom, so that their mental activities may attain understanding.

If there are those who, being there, do not hear this Dharma of the Four Truths, they shall likewise receive the eye, receive dhyāna, receive wisdom, and receive awakening, so that their minds may attain liberation. These constitute the four truths in three turnings, totaling twelve aspects; for one who knows them but has not yet attained purity, I do not grant [the fruit].

Among all the worlds—whether devas, humans, Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, or brahmins—those who have realized it through their own direct knowledge and practice the cultivation of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the vision and knowledge of liberation; these constitute the four ultimates.
"Once born hereafter, there shall be no further existence; forever separated from the world, there shall be no more sorrow or affliction.
When the Buddha spoke these words, the venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya and eighty thousand koṭis of devas all became free from dust and defilement, and the Dharma-eye was born within them.

Those thousand bhikṣus, their outflows exhausted and minds liberated, all attained arhatship; furthermore, all those higher habitual tendencies that ought to have been extinguished were entirely transformed.

The World-Honored One turned the wheel of Dharma three times, and its sound was heard everywhere by all those in the heavens and the world who stood upon the ground of the Dharma, reaching as far as the first four heavenly kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and throughout the Brahma realms, where it was heard in an instant.

At that time, the three thousandfold world-system of the Buddha’s realm, with its ten thousand suns and moons and twelve thousand heavens and earths, shook greatly. This was because the Buddha, the One Honored by the Multitudes, had begun at Vārāṇasī to turn the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma—which had never been turned before—illuminating countless beings and delivering all devas and humans, so that they might attain the Way through this.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, everyone was filled with great joy.
This is the *Sūtra on Turning the Wheel of Dharma* spoken by the Buddha.
